title: Monofixation Syndrome: The Subnormal Binocularity Guide
summary: Monofixation Syndrome (MFS) is a state of subnormal binocular vision characterized by a central suppression scotoma in one eye despite peripheral fusion. Often presenting as a 'stable' endpoint of strabismus surgery, it requires precise diagnostic testing to differentiate from bifoveal fixation.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Monofixation Syndrome (MFS), first described by Marshall Parks in 1969, is a condition where binocularity exists without bifoveal fixation. It is characterized by a small-angle strabismus (usually <8-10 prism diopters), a central suppression scotoma (1° to 3°) in the non-fixing eye, and preserved peripheral fusion. It serves as a clinically stable 'functional cure' in many strabismus cases.

rows: Post-operative result of infantile esotropia repair
Blurred foveal image leads to suppression

sections.title: The 4-Diopter Base-Out Prism Test
content: Step 1: Patient fixates on a distant target.
Step 2: Place a 4PD Base-Out prism over the suspected monofixating eye.
Step 3: Observe for an 'adjustment' movement. In MFS, the eye will NOT move because the image remains within the central scotoma.
Step 4: Place prism over the FIXING eye; both eyes will shift (Version), but the monofixating eye will not perform a secondary 'vergence' movement.

rows: Target image falls entirely within the small central scotoma

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Stereopsis: Gross only (60 to 3000 arcsec); never fine (<40 arcsec).
Cover Test: May show a small manifest tropia (Microtropia) or only a phoria (Monofixation Phoria).
Visual Acuity: Usually 20/20 to 20/50 in the non-dominant eye (mild amblyopia).
Bagolini Lenses: Symmetrical cross but with a central gap in one line (scotoma).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & High-Yield Facts
content: MFS is the 'ideal' outcome for infantile esotropia surgery (Stability).
Patients rarely complain of diplopia due to the suppression scotoma.
The scotoma size is typically 1 to 3 degrees (2 to 6 prism diopters).
If stereopsis is better than 40 arc-seconds, MFS is excluded.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Correct Refractive Error: Full cycloplegic refraction.
2. Amblyopia Therapy: Patching or Atropine if acuity is asymmetric.
3. Observe Stability: Monitor for increases in deviation size.
4. Surgery: NOT indicated for the micro-angle; only if the latent component breaks down into a large manifest tropia.

sections.title: Red Flags: When it's NOT MFS
content: Presence of Fine Stereopsis (<40 arcsec)
Diplopia (Suggests lack of suppression scotoma)
Large Angle Strabismus (>10 PD)
Rapidly worsening visual acuity (Look for organic maculopathy)

content.explanation: S: Scotoma (Central); C: Cover test (Small or no shift); A: Anisometropia (Common); L: Low Stereopsis (Gross); P: Peripheral Fusion (Present).

Diplopia: Two separate lines, no crossing

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: ELIS (Early Lens Insertion Study): Highlighted the role of early correction in preventing MFS.
Bifoveal Fixation Recovery: Recent studies suggest limited plasticity to regain bifoveal fixation in adults with MFS.
OCT Imaging: Used to ensure 'Organic MFS' is not present by ruling out subtle epiretinal membranes or macular holes.

sections.title: Prognosis & Long-term Stability
sections.content: MFS is considered one of the most stable forms of binocular alignment. Patients with secondary MFS after esotropia surgery have a significantly lower rate of recurrence (re-operation) compared to those who achieve no binocularity. It is a functional success even if it is not an anatomical 'perfect' alignment.
